column1: What is the compression ratio and why does raising it increase thermal efficiency?
column2: The ratio of cylinder volume at bottom dead center to volume at top dead center. Higher ratios compress the air-fuel charge into a smaller volume before ignition, raising peak cylinder pressures/temperatures and extracting more work per combustion event — until detonation limits become a risk.

column1: What causes engine detonation (knock) and how does the engine protect itself from it?
column2: Detonation is uncontrolled autoignition of end-gas regions ahead of the propagating flame front, destroying pistons/heads within seconds. Piezoelectric knock sensors detect the high-frequency ringing signature, and the ECU retards ignition timing in real-time, sacrificing peak power to preserve mechanical integrity.

column1: State the imperial horsepower-torque-RPM equation and what it reveals conceptually.
column2: P = (T × ω) / 5252, where P is horsepower, T is torque in lb-ft, and ω is engine speed in RPM. It reveals that power is torque delivered rapidly — the same torque at higher RPM yields proportionally more power.

column1: Why does the transmission exist in a powertrain, from a first-principles standpoint?
column2: Because the engine's useful torque band is narrow relative to the continuously varying torque demand of the car across its speed range. The transmission bridges this mismatch, letting the engine operate within its productive RPM range while wheel speed varies continuously with vehicle velocity.

column1: Give the full tractive force equation at the driven wheels and define each term.
column2: F_traction = (T_engine × i_gear × i_final × η_drivetrain) / r_wheel. T_engine = engine torque; i_gear = selected gear ratio; i_final = final drive ratio; η_drivetrain = mechanical efficiency (losses); r_wheel = dynamic rolling radius under load.

column1: Why does a lower (numerically higher) gear ratio multiply torque more but limit speed?
column2: A lower gear ratio provides greater mechanical leverage, amplifying engine torque multiple-fold at the wheel, but this trade-off caps maximum vehicle speed at a given engine RPM since wheel rotation is reduced proportionally per engine revolution.

column1: What is a typical mechanical efficiency loss range through a race-prepared sequential gearbox drivetrain?
column2: Approximately 12–18% loss from crankshaft torque to the contact patch, due to frictional and viscous losses through gear meshes and final drive.

column1: What is the distinction between sprung mass and unsprung mass in suspension analysis?
column2: Sprung mass = chassis, powertrain, and driver, supported by the springs/dampers. Unsprung mass = wheels, tires, brake assemblies, and suspension linkages, which move with the road surface below the spring/damper elements.

column1: Why does lateral weight transfer during cornering reduce total available grip, even though total vertical load is unchanged?
column2: Tire lateral force generation is nonlinear with vertical load (declining marginal return) — doubling load on the outside tire does not double its grip, while halving load on the inside tire loses more than half its contribution, so net cornering grip decreases as load transfer increases.

column1: What is the friction circle (G-G diagram) and what physical constraint does it represent?
column2: It represents the finite combined vector of longitudinal and lateral force a tire contact patch can generate, bounded by the coefficient of friction and instantaneous normal load. The combined lateral and longitudinal acceleration vector must stay within this circle or the tire exceeds grip and slides.

column1: What does a G-G scatter plot clustered near the circle's perimeter versus clustered at 60% of the envelope indicate about driver performance?
column2: Points tracing the perimeter arc indicate the driver is consistently operating near the limit of available grip; points clustered well inside the circle (e.g., at 60%) indicate the driver is leaving performance on the table, not extracting maximum combined grip.

column1: Why do racing tires and carbon brake discs require specific thermal operating windows to function correctly?
column2: Below minimum temperature, the rubber compound (or carbon-carbon brake matrix) remains too stiff to generate full molecular adhesion/friction coefficient. Above the thermal ceiling, the compound degrades irreversibly (blistering, graining, pad fade, fluid vaporization), altering contact patch geometry and reducing performance.
